How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

According to recent reports, introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

In a recent development, AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

In a recent development, an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

Industry observers note that but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky swiftly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

In a recent development, to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

According to recent reports, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Sources indicate that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

In a recent development, consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the manufacturer judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Industry observers note that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Sources indicate that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 20, 2026 at 3:05PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Oklo ›.

Many stocks related to the AI boom trade at premium valuations. Some, however, have seen their rich valuations cut in half or more this year. Oklo (OKLO -4.75%) is one of them.

Oklo specializes in small modular reactors, or SMRs. These nuclear energy facilities can be built more promptly than conventional nuclear power plants. Their small size also allows them to be co-located next to AI data center infrastructure.

AI is energy-intensive. To avoid grid reliance, AI companies have invested aggressively to scale additional energy supply. Meta Platforms (META -5.93%), for example, is partnering with Oklo on a 1.2 gigawatt SMR system in Ohio.

Despite the 70% slide in 2026, Wall Street remains upbeat on Oklo stock. No analysts currently have a "sell" rating on the stock. Several have price targets that predict more than 100% upside potential.

It has been revealed that but here's the thing: I'm still not buying Oklo shares. And there's one reason why.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

I am a major fan of SMRs as a technology. Research from Bank of America suggests that SMRs will play a role in the world's long-term energy landscape.

The problem is that SMR scaling will likely take decades. That makes Oklo a suspect investment, even at today's prices.

Industry observers note that oklo's business model doesn't just include manufacturing SMR systems. The company also intends to own and operate the assets. That may create more long-term revenue and profit potential. But it also makes Oklo's business model more capital-intensive.

In a recent development, analysts don't expect Oklo to generate positive operating income until 2031 or 2032. That means the company will need to raise new capital for years to come. While shares are cheaper after the correction, it is now harder -- or at least more onerous for existing shareholders -- for Oklo to raise more money.

Industry observers note that oklo is in a strange position as an investment candidate. As shares get cheaper, it actually becomes harder for the tech giant to finance itself -- something it will likely need to do for the rest of the decade. For that reason, I'm sticking to the sidelines for now.

    The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

    Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

    In a recent development, A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller owners also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

    The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

    According to recent reports, liberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

    For a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

    It has been revealed that there are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

    The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

    Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

    LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

    In a recent development, bundles add another option. The Omni Pro Standard Bundle includes the chair and a footrest for $983. The Maxis Electric Premium Bundle includes the chair, a footrest, and an extra battery for $1,202, down from a listed MSRP of $2,086.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that whatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

    While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp consumers: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

    If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

    Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

    According to the website, the new limit is rolling out to customers on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”.

    Recent findings suggest that whatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the revision becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

    It has been revealed that this rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the manufacturer confirmed four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

    Segway E3 Go review: A solid midrange scooter

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.
    • Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
    • Industry observers note that sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Segway E3 Go is a comfortable scooter with front suspension, but it's outshone by the E3 Pro, which can be had for just $50 more, as well as the Apollo Dash, which has a rougher ride, but is better on hills.

    Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

    Industry observers note that sometimes, you don’t need a monster of an electric scooter to get where you need to go. The Segway E3 Go is made for those with more modest demands for their commute; priced at $649 — but often on sale for less — it also places a more modest demand on your wallet.

    I rode the Segway E3 Go for a couple of weeks to get a feel for this mid-range commuter scooter, and to see how it compared to some of the best electric scooters I’ve tested over the years.

    It has been revealed that the Segway E3 Go came out in 2026, and retails for $649, though you can often find it on sale for less than $500. For example, for Black Friday, it's discounted to $449 right now.

    Segway has put a lot of thought into the feel of its scooters; in recent years, it’s started bending its handlebars slightly back, like on a bike, which gave me a bit more control while I was out and about.

    The E3 Go’s deck is also fairly spacious; unless you have gigantic feet, you should have no trouble positioning yourself on the scooter.

    I’m also a fan of the E3 Go’s folding mechanism; there’s a small tab at the base of the downtube, which you simply press with your foot to unlock the front half of the scooter and fold it down.

    Recent findings suggest that however, you’ll still need a bit of strength to carry it around, as the E3 Go weighs a meaty 46 pounds. The E3 Pro, which has dual suspension and a longer range, is actually six pounds lighter.

    Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

    In a recent development, while it lacks the full suspension of its more expensive siblings like the E3 Pro, the Go still has a front suspension. It made for a much smoother ride when going over potholes and other bumps when compared with scooters that lacked such amenities.

    Built into the handlebars of the E3 Go are turn signals, which you activate using a thumb switch on the left handlebar; I’ve loved this addition to all electric scooters I’ve tested. I just wish the E3 Go had rear turn signals, like the Segway Max G3 Plus, as it’s hard for cars behind you to see the handlebar signals. I also wish that the E3 Go’s headlight were slightly bigger, and that you could adjust its angle.

    Like most of Segway’s scooters, the E3 Go has Apple FindMy, so you can track it if it goes missing. You should always use a lock, but it’s an extra bit of protection.

    The 400W motor in the E3 Go proved good, but not great, at climbing hills. On a moderate 5% grade, the scooter slowed to around 10 MPH, which is respectable given its price; however, on a steeper hill with a 6.9% grade — which gets as steep as 10.8% — the E3 Go barely made it to the top, where the similarly-priced Apollo Dash made it up without issue. To be fair, Segway indicates that the E3 Go is rated to a max grade of 9% (18º slope).

    According to recent reports, segway advertises the E3 Go as having a max range of 25 miles; if you set the scooter to its highest performance setting, that estimate drops to just 11.2 miles. I took the E3 Go out for a 5.5-mile ride, and at its conclusion it had 32% battery life remaining, which would mean I would have made it to a little over 8 miles before the battery was completely drained. Of course, your mileage will literally vary based on your weight and the type of riding you do.

    The Segway E3 Go is a good, capable scooter for the price. It should be especially useful in flatter urban areas, and will suit commuters well, so long as you don’t have any major hills to climb. If you have steeper terrain, I would recommend the Apollo Dash; while its ergonomics aren’t as good, it has more power than the Segway, and costs about the same, with many other similar features.

    According to recent reports, if you can spring for the extra $50, the Segway E3 Pro has dual suspension and a longer range than the E3 Go, and is just as comfortable to ride. Either way, if you have to contend with a lot of potholes, the Segway and its suspension is worth a second look.

    By Leo Sun – Nov 20, 2026 at 3:10PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Bitcoin ›.

    According to recent reports, many cryptocurrencies fizzled out this year as the macro headwinds drove investors toward more conservative, higher-yielding investments. That pressure could persist over the next year as the Iran war continues, interest rates rise, and Treasury yields remain high.

    Over the next few years, many of the smaller altcoins could fade away. However, several of the top cryptocurrencies should survive that wash-out and head higher as more catalysts kick in. Let's see why three of those tokens -- Bitcoin (BTC -5.66%), Solana (SOL -5.97%), and LINK (LINK -5.08%) -- could generate much bigger gains through 2030.

    It has been revealed that bitcoin, the world's most valuable cryptocurrency, is still mined using powerful computing hardware with the energy-intensive proof-of-work (PoW) consensus mechanism. Every four years, those mining rewards are cut in half in scheduled "halvings". More than 20 million Bitcoins have already been mined, and the last token should be mined by 2140.

    CRYPTO · As of 8:08 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Bitcoin's scarcity makes it more comparable to gold and silver than other smaller tokens. But it's also easier to hold in fractional amounts and transfer than those precious metals, making it a potential hedge against expansionary monetary policies and the debasement of fiat currencies.

    Industry observers note that bitcoin's first spot-price ETFs were approved in 2024, and it should continue to gain more retail and institutional investors if the macro environment warms up again. Its next halving in 2028 will be a major catalyst, and more corporations and governments could accumulate more Bitcoins as an alternative to softening fiat currencies over the next few years.

    Solana, like Ethereum (ETH -7.23%), is a developer-oriented, proof-of-stake (PoS) blockchain that supports staking (locking up tokens to earn interest-like rewards) and smart contracts (for developing decentralized applications and other tokenized assets).

    Recent findings suggest that however, its Layer 1 (L1) blockchain processes transactions at much faster speeds than Ethereum's L1 blockchain. It achieves those higher speeds through its proprietary proof-of-history (PoH) consensus mechanism, which timestamps transactions before they're validated.

    CRYPTO · As of 8:11 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Solana's higher speeds drew in many software developers and major financial companies such as Circle (NASDAQ:CRCL), Visa (V -0.09%), PayPal (PYPL -5.46%), and Stripe -- all of which are using its blockchain to settle stablecoin transfers, tokenize real-world assets (RWAs), launch fresh cryptocurrencies, and accelerate their own financial transactions. Solana's token is used to fund those transaction fees, so the expansion of that economy makes it more valuable.

    According to recent reports, solana has already grown into the second-largest developer-driven blockchain after Ethereum, and its first spot price ETFs were approved last year. But it's still often lumped together with smaller altcoins rather than "blue chip" tokens like Bitcoin and Ethereum. I believe that perception could change by the end of the decade and drive its price much higher.

    LINK is the native token of Chainlink, the largest decentralized oracle network. An oracle network relies on independent node operators to fetch real-world data -- such as news headlines, weather reports, stock tickers, sports scores, and shipping updates -- and feed that information to developer-oriented blockchains like Solana and Ethereum. The developers on those blockchains use that data to build decentralized apps.

    CRYPTO · As of 8:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Sources indicate that chainlink allows its node operators to stake their LINK tokens as collateral to earn rewards. But if they feed false information into the oracle network, those tokens can be confiscated, and their reputation scores (essential for attracting new requests) will be reduced.

    Industry observers note that chainlink is already helping major financial institutions -- including UBS (UBS -3.78%), JPMorgan (JPM -3.03%), and Euroclear -- accelerate their blockchain transactions and tokenize RWAs. It's also modernizing financial platforms -- such as SWIFT (for interbank transfers) and the DTCC (for U.S. stock trades) -- and streamlining their settlements. As that ecosystem grows, LINK should attract more attention and become even more valuable. The first Chainlink ETFs were already launched last year, and they could attract more investors through 2030.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that with the NBA season hitting the one-month mark, let's hand out some early awards!
    • Kelly Iko: Victor Wembanyama, with a sliiiight edge over Luka Dončić.
    • At this check-in, I have to go with Dončić after a month full of a variety pack of stepback 3s.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that with the NBA season hitting the one-month mark, let's hand out some early awards! Who has been the most valuable player so far? The best rookie? The league's breakout star? Our writers weigh in with their picks.

    Kelly Iko: Victor Wembanyama, with a sliiiight edge over Luka Dončić. Of players that have registered at least 300 minutes so far, the Spurs are 42.5 points per 100 possessions better with him on the floor, the most impactful in the league by some distance. (San Antonio looked like a fish out of water earlier this week when he was on the bench vs. Detroit.) He's also realized that, at 7-foot-4, his rim presence should be consistently weaponized. Per Second Spectrum, Wemby logged 65 alley-oop dunk attempts all of last season; he's at 40 before Thanksgiving. Add this growth to his continued defensive wizardry, along with taking care of the ball and improving as a creator, and you have yourself a solid argument.

    (Dillon Minshall/Yahoo Sports illustration).

    Steve Jones: Luka Dončić. At this check-in, I have to go with Dončić after a month full of a variety pack of stepback 3s. That's 38 points a night with defenses attempting to throw multiple schemes at him and it just hasn't mattered a ton yet. Combine that with him "doing his job" on defense, with more activity on switches and rotations; he's a significant reason why the Lakers are at the top of the West.

    Recent findings suggest that dan Devine: Luka Dončić. I'm with Steve, give me the league's leading scorer, the reason the Lakers have been consistently vying for the No. 1 offense in the NBA, and the driving force behind an L.A. team that couldn't get out of the first round last year being neck-and-neck with the conference champion Spurs and East-leading 76ers for the league's best record. For more information, consult your local library:.

    According to recent reports, nekias Duncan: Victor Wembanyama. I don't think you can go wrong with Dončić or Wembanyama, honestly, but 28-12-3-1-4 on 62 true shooting is absolutely nuts. Wemby's dunking everything in sight, making teams pay when they send help — his assist rate has risen, while his turnover rate has dropped from last year — and he's pretty easily been the most destructive defender in basketball this year. The "off" portion of Wemby's on-off numbers are insane, but I'd redirect to the "on" portion — the Spurs are outscoring teams by over 28 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor.

    It has been revealed that duncan: Cameron Boozer. With all due respect to Yaxel Lendeborg and Darius Acuff Jr. (don't let them boo you, substantial dawg), I'll also be rolling with Mr. Boozer. I've been enamored with his processing speed and versatility all year long. He attacks or passes ahead of tilted defenses at a high level already. He's also showcased a willingness to let it fly from deep, a necessary buffer while he gets comfortable with his inside-the-arc work (he's converting 60% of his 2s over his last six games) against bigger players.

    According to recent reports, jones: Cameron Boozer. Rookie of the Year is going to continue to heat up as this season goes on, but Boozer's versatility offensively has delivered consistent impact for the Grizzlies. His ability to playmake fits right in with their identity: he can punish switches, and he can make plays on the short roll. There has rarely been a game where he hasn't left an imprint for a Grizzlies team that just keeps winning.

    In a recent development, devine: Yaxel Lendeborg. I'm firmly on the record as very on-board for Boozer, who became the second-youngest player in NBA history to record a triple-double, but I'll give a shout out to Lendeborg. Yes, it's been a pretty brutal week for him, and for the Warriors as a whole, since Stephen Curry went down. But what he demonstrated in his first dozen games as a pro was truly eye-opening. Coming out of Michigan, the book on Yaxel was that, as a 24-year-old super-duper-senior, he'd have the experience, toolkit and physical maturity to be able to immediately fill a role in the league. I'm not sure anyone saw that role being "guy who can average an efficient 20-plus a night on high usage, and help elevate a team that just about everybody thought was drawing dead." That might not last forever, especially if Steph's absence stretches. But for the first month, it was an exceedingly pleasant surprise.

    Iko: Darius Acuff Jr. I'm not going to punish Acuff for being born into the Kings family. I'm also not going to magnify his low shot-making efficiency or assist-to-usage ratio in Sacramento. This kid is an absolute terror with the ball in his hands, averaging 26.2 points, 7.0 assists and 3.6 rebounds a night. In spite of Sacramento. You wanna know the list of folks to achieve benchmarks like that as a rookie? Wilt. Kareem. Jordan. Oscar Robertson. Elvin Hayes. Darius. His feel for the game, creation and scoring versatility is there — the rough edges will smoothen out as time goes on.

    Jones: Memphis Grizzlies. While the Sixers keep finding ways to win as they figure it out, and while the Lakers are at the top of the West, and the Wolves have stayed steady without Anthony Edwards, the Grizzlies being one game out of the top is something few saw coming. They are 8-0 on the road, which is not just the best road start in franchise history, but the longest road winning streak in franchise history. Let that sink in.

    Duncan: Houston Rockets, if for no other reason than to save you all from the massive victory lap I'd like to take over the Grizzlies. It's not a surprise that the Rockets are a good team; the way they've been good is simply not what I had on the bingo card. They have the league's best offense and a top-five half-court unit to boot — a notable shift from last year (7th overall, 19th in the half-court). This largely hasn't been the Kevin Durant show; this is the second lowest scoring (21.3) and lowest shot-taking (13.3 attempts) season of his career. The growth and empowerment of Alperen Şengün and Amen Thompson, the confidence and shot-making of Jabari Smith Jr. (career-best 38.8% from 3), and the return of the steady-handed Fred VanVleet has led to a more efficient, free-flowing offense.

    Recent findings suggest that iko: Houston Rockets. They have very quietly made a compelling case for being a top-5 team in the NBA. VanVleet's return has come with less control than he's accustomed to, but when you're converting shots at the highest efficiency of your career, who cares about usage rates? Smith is more confident in his in-between game and still has a knack for timely momentum-shifting splashes — as well as an unheralded five-position defensive skill set. They are second in offense and seventh in defense, don't turn the ball over, obliterate opponents on the offensive glass and still have a healthy Durant. Why couldn't they stick around until June?

    Devine: Portland Trail Blazers, in part because I'm an incorrigible shill who wants to deliver a ruthless plug for the massive story he just wrote on Damian Lillard, and in part because I'm not sure anybody saw Portland sitting at 10-5 with a top-10 defense heading into opening night. Micah Nori's done a sensational job, Donovan Clingan and Toumani Camara look like bona fide linchpins, Jrue Holiday is always just what the doctor ordered, and Scoot Henderson even broke out against the Bucks on Thursday. Get Ja Morant back on the court, and Portland might just have a stew goin'.

    Devine: Toronto Raptors. It's not a shock to me that they are 5-10, given the myriad injuries they've suffered — most notably, obviously, getting just two games out of Kawhi Leonard before he went down with amorphous, ill-defined knee woes that, in a recent report by the great Michael Grange of Sportsnet, evoked the phrase "mystery condition." (Who could have foreseen this?!?) I do find it disappointing, though, that a team that won 46 games with the point differential of a 50-win squad and a top-seven defense last season — without Leonard — has so often looked so feckless this season … and that it's a combined 0-8 against teams with .500 or better records, getting blitzed by 11.5 points per 100 possessions against opponents with top-10 net ratings. Maybe, with better health, the Raptors will turn things around. Right now, though, even given the absence of their big-ticket offseason acquisition, they seem disappointingly unserious.

    Iko: Charlotte Hornets. There's no way you could have convinced me the Hornets would be 28th in net rating a week before Thanksgiving. I know the injuries to Kon Knueppel and Coby White have delayed what should have been a smooth start. But there's just something off about them when you watch, a level of disharmony and disjointedness that shouldn't be there this early in a season. Their collapse this week on the road in L.A., a game in which they led quite comfortably by 18 points deep into the second half, was embarrassing. The erasure of Brandon Miller, who has suddenly turned into a hybrid of Monta Ellis and J.R. Smith, is also jarring. Charles Lee has quite the tall task on his hands.

    In a recent development, duncan: Utah Jazz, by default. Injuries have simply derailed this group. The playmaking and screening chops of Jusuf Nurkić were missing to begin the year, an underrated hit to what the Jazz want to establish. More pressing, they've had to navigate absences from Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen. It's led to an offense that has felt rudderless at times — and easy to switch against — paired with a defense that isn't good enough to hold things together. I simply didn't think this would be a three-win team a month in.

    Jones: Cleveland Cavaliers. Per NBA.com, they are the No. 4 scoring team in the league (118.3), boasting the No. 5 offensive rating in the league (117.5), and it doesn't feel like it at all. For a team with this level of firepower, with the added bonus of continuity after an Eastern Conference finals run, the drink has felt flatter than usual. The Cavs likely just need a quick chat with momentum to turn things around, but I had high expectations for this group to take off or figure things out quickly. It has felt stuck in the middle to me.

    Recent findings suggest that iko: Paul George. If this is intended for younger players, I apologize, but I'm in complete awe of what 36-year-old is doing right now in Boston. He's played next to Jayson Tatum for only a month, but their synergy screams of a lifelong partnership. He's still firing off eight 3s a night while converting them at the highest clip of his career; still serving as an effective secondary creator, scorer and connective tissue for MazzullaBall; and still one of the premier contest-without-fouling wings around. This was supposed to be a puzzling Celtics transaction, remember? Not acquiring a player nearing 40 who's still producing at a top-25 level. Color me shocked.

    Industry observers note that jones: Davion Mitchell. Just the term breakout star had me in a headlock; I wanted to go with KAT, but he's already broken out, Cooper Flagg has taken a leap, Franz Wagner is scoring and playmaking, and LaMelo Ball is playing defense. I'm going with Mitchell, leaning on the breakout portion of the program. He's been dynamic in transition and in pick-and-roll, finding his way into the paint consistently. The on-ball pressure remains tremendous and he's knocking down 3s. He's been exactly what the Heat have needed.

    Sources indicate that duncan: Cedric Coward. (Davion Mitchell is such a tremendous shout!) Coward has simply been awesome for the Grizzlies to start the year. He's shooting the leather off the ball (45.2% on 5.2 attempts from 3), the drives have more juice, the passing has perked up, and he continues to add value as an offensive rebounder. On the other end, he's putting together a legitimate All-Defense campaign while consistently taking on tough assignments. As of this writing, opposing offenses are generating under 0.8 points per possession whenever Coward defends a ball screen (0.76), a handoff (0.76), or an off-ball screen (0.55). There's a reason the Grizzlies have been nearly 15 points better per 100 possessions with him on the floor.

    Industry observers note that devine: Holy crap, none of you guys stated Ty Jerome? OK, then: Ty freaking Jerome!

    Sources indicate that there are five players in the NBA this season averaging at least 25 points and five assists per game on .600 true shooting, and Ty Jerome is the only one of them that 99% of NBA fans couldn't pick out of a lineup. (The other four: Luka, Giannis, Tyrese Maxey, Jamal Murray.) Sickos who do this for a living might have been aware that the eighth-year pro out of Virginia could be capable of this sort of production given health and opportunity, but it's certainly come as a shock to just about everybody else — including opponents of the Grizzlies who might've come into the season expecting things to be sweet only to find themselves on the business end of a steady diet of impossible floaters and 30-foot pull-up bombs. Memphis has been one of the best stories in the league this season, and its low-profile, high-octane point guard has been one of the biggest reasons why.

    iOS 27.3: Newly introduced features, release date, more

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta users.
    • 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off.
    • According to recent reports, as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone people sometime in December.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta users. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

    9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

    According to recent reports, as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone people sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

    Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

    So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

    The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final enhancement.

    The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

    For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 customers, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

    Industry observers note that for Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a upcoming Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

    As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

    For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

    Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

    It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

    iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

    Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a upcoming option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

    When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

    Industry observers note that this includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

    In a recent development, iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many fresh capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

    We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

    Recent findings suggest that there are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

    It has been revealed that with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

    According to recent reports, today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

    While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple indicates it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

    iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to fresh languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

    Sources indicate that iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

    In a recent development, you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ proposal, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

    It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

    In a recent development, iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

    iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

    For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

    The revision also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

    In a recent development, there are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

    Second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a new “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

    #27988. Latest Update: Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (948 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
    • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
    • It has been revealed that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the organization’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

    Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

    It has been revealed that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

    It has been revealed that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

    (If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

    In a recent development, I’m a substantial fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, owners should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

    However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy people at least would like a little more transparency and control.

    AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, customers had to wait until it “just worked.”.

    Recent findings suggest that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an patch, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

    Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

    According to recent reports, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

    It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

    According to recent reports, will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

    Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

    In a recent development, I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech customers may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

    Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it.
    • When you need to create a upcoming event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc.
    • According to recent reports, in iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

    When you need to create a upcoming event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

    According to recent reports, in iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

    While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

    Sources indicate that apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

    With Siri AI, that’s changed in a major way. Now, you can do things like:.

    According to recent reports, popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a upcoming update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

    Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

    As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t right now provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

    By default, owners who patch and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. People who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the newly introduced toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

    Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

    Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a latest toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

    Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

    Industry observers note that prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

    It has been revealed that it’s good to see that customers can manually disable the latest privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise key questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

    Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this enhancement.

    What do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

    iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

    When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were unveiled in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

    Sources indicate that the idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

    Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:.

    Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

    Industry observers note that before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

    According to recent reports, in iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

    That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

    Sources indicate that the only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

    Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.
