    Glass House Brands (GLAS -2.48%) reported third quarter revenue of $56.8 million and record biomass production of 319,000 pounds while navigating an unfavorable product mix and wholesale price compression. Management reported that the firm completed the deconsolidation of its retail operations and successfully uplisted to the New York Stock Exchange during the period. Operational focus remains on optimizing Greenhouse 2 and Greenhouse 5 to improve the ratio of high-value flower and smalls in the production mix. The company reported a cash balance of $39.7 million, which management stated is sufficient to fund its $20 million capital expenditure plan and reach positive cash flow. Strategic initiatives include preparing for potential interstate and international commerce following the transition of medical cannabis to Schedule III and obtaining international quality certifications for existing farms.

    Operator: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to the Glass House Brands Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Matters discussed during today's conference call may constitute forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties relating to Glass House Brands' future financial or business performance. Actual results could differ materially from those anticipated in those forward-looking statements. The risk factors that may affect results are detailed in Glass House Brands' periodic filings and registration statement. I'd also like to remind everyone that this call is being recorded today, Monday, November 16, 2026. On today's call, we have Kyle Kazan, Co-Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; and Mark Vendetti, Chief Financial Officer. Also joining for questions is Graham Farrar, Co-Founder and President.

    It has been revealed that and with that, I'll turn the call over to Kyle Kazan. Please go ahead.

    Kyle Kazan: Thank you, operator. First, I'll be discussing Glass House Brands' recent financial performance, along with the company activities. Then our CFO, Mark Vendetti, will share the financials, after which I will wrap up before the 3 of us take your questions. As the Co-Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer since day 1, I'm one of the key architects of how our company was built and who we are today. Since that day, Glass House Brands was built to be a company for the future for the day when California cannabis would be legally accessible to consumers around the country and the world.

    Recent findings suggest that however, we have been prepared and still are to succeed completely within the confines of our state until the walls come down and we are allowed to ship across our borders. We are well positioned as the Golden State has the beautiful California sunshine, appellation due to generations of legacy growers who created amazing strains and the most discerning consumers of this wonderful plant. At Glass House, we are the largest cultivator on the planet, owning 6 million square feet of greenhouses. We have not turned on our entire footprint and still have room to expand when we can sell outside of California.

    Industry observers note that even though harnessing mother nature is not always easy, I proudly stand by the decision today to be a greenhouse grower in California as most cannabis grown around the country is being done in warehouses at multiples more expensive than our costs. But the road not travel is certainly not easy as evidenced by our recent financial performance. As most of you know, pricing in California has been challenging when compared to other markets. As such, the average price outside of California is far higher than it is within our state. When interstate commerce becomes the reality, California pricing will improve and consumers in higher-priced states will get relief.

    Recent findings suggest that the net effect, we believe, will be substantially higher pricing than what we are currently seeing in California. To that end, since medicinal cannabis became Schedule III, a company priority has been to work closely at the highest levels with the California Department of Cannabis Control, or the DCC. Our consultant, Matt Murphy of Pharma Compliance Group, is working with both the DCC and the Drug Enforcement Administration to understand how we can access other markets as soon as possible. Although interstate commerce is not currently a reality, we will remain focused given its importance to Glass House and consumers everywhere.

    According to recent reports, as we look outside of California, in October, we received Good Agriculture and Collection Practice, GACP certifications for our Casitas and Padaro farms from Perry Johnson Registrars Food Safety. These certifications confirm that the facilities meet the strict international and interstate safety and quality standards required for medical cannabis markets, and they represent a critical step towards supplying those markets both domestically and internationally once export is permitted. Together, the 2 farms comprise more than 0.5 million square feet of advanced greenhouse cultivation, making them amongst the largest GACP-certified facilities in the United States. Markets such as Germany, the U.K. and Switzerland require GACP-compliant operations.

    In a recent development, so these certifications expand our pathway to higher-priced medicinal markets and a meaningful larger addressable opportunity as regulatory environment continues to evolve. Now turning to our third quarter results. Third quarter revenue was $56.8 million. We produced 319,000 pounds of biomass during the quarter, a record for the company and ahead of the 246,000 pounds produced last quarter. Third quarter cost of production was $109 a pound compared to the $122 per pound reported in the second quarter of 2026 and $175 per pound in the first quarter. This marks more than a 37% cost production improvement since the first quarter.

    It has been revealed that the improvement comes from continued operational efficiency enhancement as our workforce gains experience every day, and we benefit from higher production volume across a larger footprint. We remain on track to produce approximately 1 million pounds of biomass this year and exit the year with cost of production around our current level with our long-term target of $95 per pound intact. In the second quarter of 2026, it became clear that we were growing less flower and smalls and more trim. The trim mix glitch persisted into the third quarter, and our CFO estimates it cost us in excess of $10 million.

    As such, our average selling price for the quarter was $151 per pound, down from $211 per pound last quarter. Let me address this decrease directly. The ASP is the combination of 3 main factors: the trim mix we sold, the yields we achieved on flower and smalls and the underlying market. The largest driver this quarter was mix. We sold a higher proportion of trim, roughly 63% of pounds sold versus the high 40s and low 50s we saw in prior periods and well above our historical best of around 45%. Flower and smalls together made up only about 37% of sales.

    In a recent development, in 2024, for comparison, flower alone was closer to 37% in that quarter, and our 2027 projections target a meaningfully better mix. Part of this is timing. As we finished the second quarter with higher inventory levels than expected, we sold more inventory in the third quarter from earlier production periods that were more trim-heavy. The production mix improved during the quarter, and we expect further improvement in the fourth quarter. Because of the normal lag between harvest and sale, the sales mix in any given quarter does not fully reflect the production improvements already underway. Production quality and mix better indicate where we are heading.

    According to recent reports, had we sold the mix that we actually produced during the quarter, the ASP would have been higher at today's prices at $180 a pound, about $29 higher per pound than we had achieved. As previously stated, the market is a factor as well. Flower pricing in the second quarter of '26 was actually slightly higher than the prior year. However, in the third quarter, that reversed and flower sold in the high 300s a pound this quarter versus the low 400s a year ago. California wholesale price remains compressed relative to other markets and prior years, and we do not control that.

    It has been revealed that pricing is also subject to normal seasonal variation and has been softer in the back half of the year, consistent with historical patterns. What we do control is the mix and the yields, and those are the areas where we are focused. On the production side, flower and smalls per square foot ran below 2024 levels this summer. The drivers are similar to what we talked about last quarter. The genetics we had to plant coming out of last year's disruption, a large share of the workforce still early on the learning curve as we expanded capacity and the temporary off-line status of a cogeneration unit that limited CO2. Wetter weather in the first half also played a role.

    These are near-term concerns, not structural ones. The important point is that we are already seeing the [ turn ]. Production mix improved during the third quarter relative to the prior quarter. Operational changes, better screening, healthier plants, improved defoliation and day-to-day execution are showing up in the numbers. We are seeing an improvement in production mix and continued progress on cost of production. These operational gains are not yet fully reflected in the financial results given the timing of sales, but they give us confidence that the trajectory is improving. It's also important to note that none of the larger capital investments we already have underway or have planned are yet reflected in these results.

    Industry observers note that these investments are designed to further improve yields, mix and consistency as we move through 2027 to optimize Greenhouse 5 and 6. The capital we are deploying is directed toward facility upgrades and process improvements that are intended to improve yields, mix and to support further reductions in cost of production. We recognize that the third quarter fell short on mix and average selling price. Since last year's disruption, greater scale and the use of third-party processing have made the lag between harvest and sale less predictable than it was previously, and we are working to improve that visibility. Looking to the fourth quarter, we expect the sold mix to continue improving.

    It has been revealed that our current forecast has flower and smalls together approaching 45% of pounds sold, up from 37% in the third quarter, even as flower pricing follows its normal seasonal decline from the high 300s into the low 300s. The blended ASP may, therefore, remain soft in the fourth quarter, but the underlying production quality and mix appear to be heading in the right direction. As pricing typically strengthen seasonally in the first quarter, we should see the benefit of the improved mix more clearly. During the third quarter, we also made the decision to pause our hemp operations after determining that the results did not support continued investment at this time.

    According to recent reports, this action allows us to concentrate resources on our core cannabis cultivation business where we continue to see stronger opportunities for returns. We will remain disciplined in evaluating any future hemp-related opportunities should market conditions or the economics improve. When we're getting back on our feet during the quarter, we also turned on Greenhouse 2 which boasts 11,000 lights powered by our cogeneration facilities. Frankly, it is this greenhouse we are most excited about when we first visited the facility in October of 2018. Those lights changed seasonality compared to non-light-assisted greenhouses, and we believe they would produce some of the best quality cannabis on the planet.

    In retrospect, while our excitement about Greenhouse 2 remains, turning on another massive greenhouse while we were continuing to train and expand a new workforce took up a lot of the team's bandwidth and the focus. Given the prerelease of our third quarter earnings, where we announced that we had $39 million in cash in the balance sheet, which we believe is enough to get us to cash flow positive, I want to address some of the tools that we have to get us there. An amazingly gritty team, I have never been luckier to call a group of individuals, my long-time teammates than I am now, and I'm always amazed at how we execute even during challenging times.

    In a recent development, our preferred equity, as we created both existing rounds internally, we were deliberate that if necessary, we could forgo cash dividends and convert them to payment-in-kind. While we have never done this, it is a lever we can pull, which would save us almost $12 million over the course of the year. Our $50 million in corporate debt, we chose a sophisticated bank, which has been very supportive. They have recently granted us a waiver for an additional 4 quarters of loan covenants, given us further financial flexibility as we continue to address near-term concerns and prepare for a world with interstate commerce.

    Our deeply experienced team knows the California cannabis market inside and out, and we will make whatever changes are necessary within our organization so we have absolutely what we need to succeed. At the end of June 2027, the multiple voting shares will expire, and I do not intend to ask the Board of Directors and shareholders to extend them. I also want to briefly address my related party transactions disclosed in our filings as we know this is an area of interest for investors. As you will hear, many have already been terminated or in the process to terminate. Some of these relate to real estate leases for retail properties.

    Sources indicate that several of these properties are partially owned by me, including through Beach Front properties and related trusts. It should be noted that the retail properties have been deconsolidated from Glass House Brands and the lease obligations are with Glass House Retail. A couple of items worth highlighting. One of the retail leases with 2000 De La Vina LLC was terminated in 2025 in connection with the sale of the underlying property. Subsequent to September 30, 2026, an agreement was entered into with 2000 De La Vina LLC, under which the remaining termination payment obligations under the terminated lease would cease effective October 1, 2026.

    In August 2025, Glass House Brands acquired the remaining 76% undivided ownership interest in the Lompoc property that had been leased from Neo Street Partners. This acquisition eliminates future related party ownership and rent expense associated with that facility. In the case of the lease of our corporate headquarters, which is owned by an entity in which I have a 50% ownership stake, the lease was renewed effective January 1, 2025. In 2026, the lease was modified in favor of Glass House Brands, allowing the company to terminate at its options with 30-day notice. Glass House Brands is evaluating its office needs and is strongly considering terminating in 2027 as part of our company optimization planning.

    Outside of the leases, we had a long-standing consulting agreement with Beach Front Property Management for M&A advisory, real estate acquisition and financing service. The agreement allowed Glass House Brands to raise significant capital without using investment banks and broker-dealers, saving many millions of dollars in fees for the company. I controlled Beach Front Property Management through the Kazan Trust, which owns 51% of its parent holding company. The agreement was terminated on September 18, 2026. This termination eliminates the related party contract going forward. We have used Jon A. Neu Insurance, which is a majority owned by Beach Front Properties as a vendor for insurance brokerage services.

    When we first started the business and made these arrangements, it's important to remember that the cannabis industry was much different than it is now. Regulatory reform was nowhere near where it is today and getting insurance in cannabis was difficult. In 2026, Glass House Brands instituted a formal process to obtain request for proposals for all organization services. We expect to choose a nonrelated vendor by the end of this year. My family trust, related entities and my children's trusts are invested in the Series D preferred issuance and the E convertible preferred issuance and participate in the conversion of certain earlier series into Series E.

    In a recent development, all of these transactions were completed on the same terms and conditions as those applicable to nonrelated party holders. No preferential rights or special arrangements were provided. Full details of each arrangements, including related party rent and other expense amounts are included in the related party transactions note to our consolidated financial statements available on SEDAR. I'm happy to take questions on any of these items. Now before I turn the call over for our financial review, I'd like to recognize Mark Vendetti, who recently announced he will be retiring from his role as Chief Financial Officer at the end of March 2027. Mark is only the second CFO in Glass House's history.

    Sources indicate that and over the past 5 years, he has been a dedicated member of our executive team and a true friend to many of us, including me. He has guided the company through significant milestones, including this year's deconsolidation and New York Stock Exchange uplisting and his contributions have been important to where we stand today. We are grateful for his commitment and the work he has done. We have initiated a search for his successor. I'd also like to note that as previously unveiled, John Nichols, Jr. has resigned from our Board of Directors. We thank Jay for his service to Glass House and wish him well in his future endeavors.

    I am hyper-focused on filling these key roles, including adding independent directors for both audit and medical roles. Interviews are underway, and we will introduce latest leaders as appropriate. With that, I will turn the call over to Mark Vendetti, our Chief Financial Officer, to discuss our financial results for the quarter in detail. Mark?

    Mark Vendetti: Thank you, Kyle. Good afternoon, everyone. Before I get into the numbers, I want to note that all prior period results discussed today reflect continuing operations. As a reminder, we recast our historical results to exclude Glass House Retail following its deconsolidation on June 12, consistent with how we presented our second quarter financials. So the comparisons I'll walk through, including our third quarter 2025 figures are on the same consistent basis. Third quarter revenue was $56.8 million, up from $26.2 million in the third quarter of 2025. This is comprised of $50 million in wholesale biomass and $6.3 million in CPG sales, which compares to $21.2 million and $5 million, respectively, in the third quarter of last year.

    We produced 319,000 pounds of wholesale biomass in the third quarter, up from 246,000 pounds in the second quarter and 124,000 pounds in the third quarter of 2025. The improvements reflect continued operational efficiency gains as our workforce matures and we benefit from higher production volume across a larger footprint. This was disconcerning as the ability to complete review of 2026 transactions and filing Q3 results on time was discussed with them prior to our engagement. We found the prospect of missing a reporting deadline or not filing with an auditor's review is suggested to be unacceptable for our shareholders.

We believe their interpretation of the applicable Canadian reporting rule is wrong as no resolved issue would arise unless they completed their work and we did not agree. We were obliged to disclose BDO's position even though we believe BDO is wrong.

    Frederico Yokota Gomes: First question about the mix of trim and flower. I appreciate the color you provided there. And is there any meaningful costs associated with that, I guess, with fixing that cogen plant?

    Graham Farrar: I can take both of those. Thanks a lot for the call, Federico. So a couple of things. One is on the mix, just as a reminder, that Q3 was record production for biomass and flower. So I want to make sure that it doesn't get lost in there that the work we are doing is actually record setting. The good news is that operationally, the production leads sales.

One is operational, which we can see that we're already fixing. The other is facilities, which is where we've introduced some projects to make some improvements.

    In a recent development, we had a tough time this summer, particularly in Greenhouses 5 and 6 with their ability to cool the greenhouses, fans that weren't moving as much air as they used to, resulting in the growers trying to screen to control temperature, which hurt light and impacted yields. The next step is actually going to be to upgrade the facilities, which should get us not only back to our historical baseline, but should give us the opportunity, particularly with Greenhouse 2 to do even better than that. On your cogen question, yes, the cogen has been offline for a bit. There's 3 things that we get from the cogen.

    Recent findings suggest that one is electricity, which we used to sell and still do in the heating time, but predominantly used to run the lights in Greenhouse 2. The other thing you get from it is heat and CO2. Every one of those is valuable at a farm, which is why the cogens are so nice to have. We can make electricity at $0.08 a kilowatt instead of buying it for $0.28 and we get that free heat and the free CO2 at the same time. Now that we have the light, the cogen being down has multiple impacts, one of which is that we don't have all the power we want to turn all the lights that we want.

    And the more light we have, the better yields we have. The other, and this is something we've historically had that we've been without is the exhaust from that cogen that we put into the greenhouses and the CO2 helps improve yields. It also makes the plants more tolerant to heat. So with not being able to supplement with that CO2, it reduced the yields. The plants don't grow as fast and they grow bigger leaves rather than the bigger buds that we're after. So they just did the commissioning on that. The engine has been worn in. And if things go well sometime this week, we'll actually see it go back into service.

    Industry observers note that so we have not had any of the benefit of it up until at this moment. But hopefully, before this week is over, we will see that change. Plant growth cycle is about 60 days from there, another 30 days to process it and then a little bit of time to sell it. But as soon as we can start putting that CO2 back into the greenhouses, we will get the benefit from it and the crops that are in there will start to reflect that when they're harvested.

The timing of when they do it certainly is not something that's in our control. I think there's been quite -- there's been a lot of confusion, which I totally understand on this topic. I do think people are missing the forest for the trees a little bit. The forest is that this process is actually happening. I mean we can, at this point, say it has happened. There are now 900-plus stores federally allowed and licensed by the DEA to sell cannabis, right?

    Industry observers note that like that is a step change, a paradigm shift, 50 years of cannabis prohibition that has now at least started to end, right? Like there are stores today, as we sit here, can sell cannabis federally legally. There's a lot of questions about how does that happen in the letters that are going out. I think it's worth noting that no licenses have been rejected yet. There have been letter -- not to say they won't be, but they have not been yet. There are letters to show cause, they call them, which have been issued to some dispensaries, which also hold adult-use licenses.

The ALJ hearing hasn't concluded. So if they're applying their playbook and they don't have adult use in it, kind of what else can they say at this moment. I think the key piece there, though, is they're applying their existing playbook, right?

    They are treating cannabis as a Schedule III drug. There is no Schedule III drug that's not available in all states. There's no Schedule III drug that doesn't ship with interstate commerce. There's no Schedule III drug that doesn't have international exports. So the fact that they're applying the Schedule III rule book all the way down to the ledgers that they use to transfer the product is the key piece. The process is happening, the football is in the air. And of course, there are things that have to be worked out, right? There's no question. There's never been the opportunity to interface state and federal programs together until now. So will they get figured out?

    Yes, because now they can be. So I think it is certainly something that we're watching closely. Don't know the exact timing. But to me, it's very encouraging that there actually is a process to work on because we've been waiting 50 years for that. If the DEA maintains a stance that says any licensing program with adult use isn't eligible, the result of that would be 55% of the population is not covered. 85% of the cannabis sales are not addressed. So one way or the other, these pieces are going to get put together. I think the exciting part is that we finally have the opportunity to work on that.

    HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
    • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
    • It has been revealed that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

    HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

    It has been revealed that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

    In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

    In a recent development, “Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

    Industry observers note that in the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

    Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

    It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

    The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

    Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

    The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

    Industry News: AirPods 5 vs AirPods Pro 3: Which should you buy this holiday season?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts.
    • 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off.
    • Industry observers note that airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

    9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

    Industry observers note that airPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

    According to recent reports, the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

    Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

    The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

    It has been revealed that if you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

    If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

    For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

    It has been revealed that airPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

    AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

    I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

    If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $179. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

    In a recent development, finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

    This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

    Recent findings suggest that airPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

    According to recent reports, if you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

    #27968. Latest Update: Inkling 2 Mini

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3141 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thinkingmachines ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Inkling 2 Mini

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thinkingmachines

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.
    • It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token.
    • Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

    It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

    SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (51 tasks).

    Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

    We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

    We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

    Recent findings suggest that most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

    Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

    Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

    Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

    It has been revealed that while looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

    It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

    Sources indicate that researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance.Researchers at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab and Scaling Intelligence Lab got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini. Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B.Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

    In a recent development, efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

    Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

    Inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

    Inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations.Universal Transformers, Dehghani et al., 2018 In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

    Compute-equivalent gain by loop position.

    Our model uses attention residuals.Attention Residuals, Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026 Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

    The previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

    To evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

    It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a recent article on Connectionism. We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

    Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

    Inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

    In a recent development, after pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

    Following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

    In a recent development, A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is monitoring its chain of thought (CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

    Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

    One reason we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini is to enable the community to conduct research on looped transformers. We are particularly excited for researchers to investigate questions of monitorability, and to develop interpretability techniques for understanding the computation within loops.

    To explore how different amounts of looping affect model properties like monitorability, we also trained a variable-looped model, TML-d24-varloop-research, because Inkling 2 Mini only supports a fixed number of looping passes. To enable variable looping, TML-d24-varloop-research was trained with between one and five looping passes.TML-d24-varloop-research was primarily trained for 3 passes of looping, with lower exposure to 1, 2, 4, and 5 passes. Performance at these latter pass counts may understate what training specifically for them could achieve. See the model card for details. We have also made this model publicly available on Hugging Face.

    Below we describe our preliminary analysis of how looping affects monitorability. Overall, we find that looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning.

    As a first step, we measured how much additional reasoning looping enables by comparing looped and non-looped models of the same size on tasks answered with no CoT at all. We used Think Fast, a benchmark that estimates a model’s no-CoT time horizon: the length of task, measured in human completion time, that a model can complete at 50% reliability without using CoT.These models were not trained to answer questions without a CoT. To elicit no-CoT answers, we prefilled the start of the response so that the model must answer directly, skipping reasoning. Other elicitation techniques, such as fine-tuning, might yield higher no-CoT performance and are worth exploring.

    Recent findings suggest that as expected, looping increases no-CoT capability, though these gains eventually level off. The no-CoT time horizon of TML-d24-varloop-research rises from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three. Some of this is presumably due to the additional serial computation that looping provides. Beyond three passes, the time horizon is roughly flat. Interestingly, the model was never trained with more than five passes, and yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its performance.

    No-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds).

    Industry observers note that as the number of looped passes increases past three, the gains are smaller, and on most tasks we observe similar performance. One exception is the N-Hop Lookup task, which cleanly evaluates serial reasoning: the model is given several lookup tables with fictional entries, and must follow a chain of lookups without writing anything down. We find that the model follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops.

    Sources indicate that in standard evaluations with CoT, we observe that more loop passes primarily benefit multi-hop reasoning rather than recall. Gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), followed by math and science reasoning (HMMT, GPQA Diamond, HLE) and long-horizon agentic tasks (SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp). Closed-book factual QA is nearly invariant to loop passes (SimpleQA Verified, WorldVQA). See model card for full evaluations.

    We next measured whether a model’s CoT reveals less about its reasoning as looping increases via two evaluations. First, we assessed how looping impacts the compression and legibility of a model’s CoT. Second, we measured how controllable a model’s CoT is, i.e., whether it can deliberately reshape its CoT to satisfy constraints. For each, we run TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five looped passes to study the effect of looping.

    Note that TML-d24-varloop-research was only trained on variable pass counts from 1 to 5 during midtraining, and its RL was done with 3 passes. These experiments therefore do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively. A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work.

    Compression and legibility. Since looping allows a model to spend more compute per token, we expect that it should need fewer CoT tokens to reach the same performance. We ran the variable-looped model at 1 to 5 passes, and found that as looping increases, the model generally achieves higher accuracy at each reasoning token budget, with diminishing returns after 3 passes. Notably, token efficiency on GPQA Diamond improves slightly from 3 to 5 passes, even though the model was trained with RL only at 3 passes, suggesting that some compression comes from additional computation itself, without RL at that depth.

    Accuracy versus reasoning tokens.

    DeepSWE v1.1 Accuracy (% of tasks resolved).

    The observed CoT compression raises a question for monitorability: is shorter reasoning still readable, or does it omit crucial details about the model’s thinking? We compared traces from the variable-looped model on the GPQA Diamond questions that it answered correctly at all five pass counts. Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged. On initial analysis, the difference is that the model is more direct and backtracks less on the way to the answer. The example below illustrates this difference on a simple question.

    Sources indicate that march 1 falls on a Tuesday in a year that is not a leap year. What day of the week is May 20 of the same year? Give the final answer on its own last line as ANSWER: .

    Controllability. One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluationReasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought, Yueh-Han et al., 2026 measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

    Industry observers note that both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

    Chain-of-thought controllability.

    CoT controllability (log scale).

    Sources indicate that to measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used LinuxArena, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

    In a recent development, with the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

    Agentic monitorability will be notable to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

    The goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and important setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

    Recent findings suggest that we are working with the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided Goodfire, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings here.

    In a recent development, efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

    Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, TokenSpeed, and Llama App, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

    In a recent development, we work to empower people with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

    Apple Watch Series 12: Four standout features make me glad I upgraded

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.
    • The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.
    • I’m happy to report that the latest S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

    The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

    I’m happy to report that the latest S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

    According to recent reports, everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

    The new Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

    Because of the upcoming health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:.

    In a recent development, the complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

    I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a fresh Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

    Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

    In a recent development, most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

    Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

    More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:.

    I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off rapidly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

    Apple Watch Series 12 is now only $329 on Amazon, down from $399.

    Recent findings suggest that have you upgraded to Apple Watch Series 12? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

    By RJ Fulton – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 3:30PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.

    Industry observers note that the recent semiconductor sell-off has presented investors with potentially attractive buying opportunities as concerns surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) valuations weigh on the sector. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) and Intel (INTC -7.97%) have fallen approximately 26% and 42% from their respective recent highs.

    Recent findings suggest that AMD has established itself as a major supplier of high-performance computing products, capitalizing on growing demand for AI infrastructure. Intel, meanwhile, is pursuing an ambitious turnaround centered on restoring its competitive position in processor design and semiconductor manufacturing.

    While both companies stand to benefit from continued investment in AI, their contrasting financial performance, capital requirements, and competitive positions present two distinct investment opportunities.

    It has been revealed that AMD designs high-performance processors and accelerators for data centers, personal computers, and gaming systems. Its expanding portfolio of AI accelerators and multiyear strategic partnership with OpenAI position the tech giant to capture a greater share of AI infrastructure spending. Meanwhile, established relationships with companies such as Sony and Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) provide additional revenue streams through its gaming business.

    In the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $45.4 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 41.9%. AMD generated $7.6 billion in net income over the same period, translating to a profit margin of roughly 16.8%. Its ability to deliver substantial revenue growth while maintaining profitability is particularly attractive as investors increasingly scrutinize the financial performance of AI-related companies.

    Sources indicate that as of December 2025, AMD maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1 and a current ratio of 2.9, reflecting a relatively strong balance sheet. The manufacturer also generated approximately $6.7 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025, although stock-based compensation accounted for 21.2% of operating cash flow.

    Sources indicate that intel designs and manufactures processors for personal computers, data centers, and networking applications. While its established processor business remains a significant source of revenue, much of Intel's long-term investment thesis centers on its foundry strategy. By expanding its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, Intel aims to compete for manufacturing contracts from other chip designers while reducing its reliance on traditional processor sales.

    Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached approximately $59.9 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 12.1%. However, Intel recorded a net loss of roughly $12 billion, translating to a negative profit margin of 20.1%. Despite improving revenue, Intel continues to face substantial financial challenges as it works to regain market share and establish a competitive semiconductor manufacturing business.

    Industry observers note that as of December 2025, Intel maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.4 and a current ratio of approximately 2.0. However, the company recorded negative free cash flow of $4.9 billion in fiscal 2025, while stock-based compensation accounted for 25.1% of operating cash flow.

    One of AMD's primary risks is intense competition from Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), which maintains an established lead in the AI accelerator market. However, geopolitical and regulatory risks are becoming increasingly significant. On Nov. 19, AMD shares fell nearly 8% following a report alleging ties to blacklisted Chinese companies, claims AMD has disputed. Upcoming U.S. export restrictions targeting remote access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centers could also limit international growth opportunities.

    Intel faces considerably greater financial and operational risks. Unlike AMD, Intel must absorb the substantial costs of developing and operating its own semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Its foundry strategy requires significant capital investment, with profitability largely dependent on securing external manufacturing customers and achieving sufficient production volumes. Intel must accomplish this while attempting to regain market share in its traditional processor business. Customer concentration adds another layer of risk, with its three largest customers accounting for approximately 43% of net revenue in 2025.

    Intel appears to be the cheaper option based on both the Forward P/E, which compares stock price to future earnings estimates, and the P/S ratio, which measures market cap divided by sales over the past twelve months.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    In a recent development, from a valuation standpoint, Intel appears to be the more affordable option, trading at 37.2 times forward earnings compared to AMD's 60.6. Intel also trades at 4.9 times sales, considerably below AMD's multiple of 17.7. Although neither stock looks particularly cheap, I believe AMD's stronger financial position and growth prospects make it the more compelling investment following the recent semiconductor sell-off.

    Sources indicate that with interest rates remaining elevated and investors increasingly scrutinizing AI-related capital expenditures, the financial composition of each company deserves particular consideration. AMD's limited debt burden, positive free cash flow, and established profitability provide the financial flexibility to invest in product development without relying heavily on external financing. In contrast, Intel must fund an expensive manufacturing turnaround while contending with substantial losses and negative free cash flow.

    Although AMD's elevated valuation leaves it vulnerable to further selling pressure, I believe its stronger balance sheet, superior revenue growth, and considerably lower capital requirements justify a valuation premium. Given the current macroeconomic environment, I would rather invest in a semiconductor company with proven financial performance than one whose investment thesis depends heavily on a successful turnaround.

    Among iOS 27’s many latest features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

    With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting latest features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

    But the patch also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

    One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

    Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

    According to recent reports, after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

    In a recent development, to move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

    Industry observers note that most consumers will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

    If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

    So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple intends to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As you can intuit from the headline, we've got good news and bad news regarding Valve's Steam Machine.

    Recent findings suggest that first, the good news: Valve unveiled that it's worked through all of the waitlist orders for the 512GB model of the Steam Machine, and you can now purchase one for as long as supplies last. The gaming giant also finished sending out invites to the remaining reservation holders for the 2TB variant.

    This is related to the bad news, but it might take a while for Valve to fulfill 2 TB requests. There are more people on that list than there are consoles available.

    Yes, the Steam Machine is still expensive at $1,049, but it is finally available outside of a wishlist. Despite the price and somewhat underpowered specs, it is well-designed hardware and brings Steam OS to your couch. It's awesome for indie titles, older games and emulation.

    The announcement post revealed that the company is still fighting supply constraints for hardware components, an ongoing consequence of RAMageddon.

    Recent findings suggest that "Even when we are able to build more, it will be at smaller quantities than we planned," the post reads. The organization is also closing new signups for the waitlist.

    Also, it's not clear how many 512GB Steam Machines are available for purchase. Instead of creating another waitlist, Valve notes it will mark the model as out of stock.

    Fortunately, as we found in September, a little hack can greatly expand your storage, so the 512GB version isn't as dire as you may think.

    Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

    Recent findings suggest that the Steam Machine is already more expensive than Valve wanted to price it, but high prices for RAM and storage changed the company's looks. Right now, the 512GB version starts at $1,049, while the 2TB model starts at $1,349.

    Valve once again highlighted that "memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels" in this week's post.

    Sources indicate that "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them," the company wrote. "The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.".

    It has been revealed that this suggests that a price hike is coming. Valve says that it will announce more information in January on both availability and pricing.
